facts.text: A manufacturer of heavy off-road machines for construction, mining and quarrying already sells a system that warns the operator when the machine gets too close to an object.
facts.quote: A manufacturer of heavy off-road machines for construction, mining and quarrying already sells a system that warns the operator when the machine gets too close to an object.

facts.text: The heavy off-road machine manufacturer is developing a successor to its proximity-warning system that also applies the brakes automatically if the operator does not react.
facts.quote: It is now developing a successor that also applies the brakes automatically if the operator does not react.

facts.text: The new automatic-braking system for heavy off-road machines must work on many kinds of job site, in many weather and light conditions, and on many machine models.
facts.quote: The new system must work on many kinds of job site, in many weather and light conditions, and on many machine models.

facts.text: The research aimed to ground the heavy off-road machine validation plan in actual job-site failures and operator behavior around warning and intervention systems, using knowledge as of October 2026.
facts.quote: set out to ground the validation plan in what actually goes wrong on job sites and in how operators behave around warning and intervention systems, as of October 2026.

facts.text: The research was to examine accident and incident data from mine safety and workplace safety agencies in several countries to characterize heavy mobile machine collisions by who or what is hit, machine type, movement, speed, site type, light and weather. Movements to examine included reversing, driving forward, turning and swinging.
facts.quote: who or what is hit, by which machine types, in which movement (reversing, driving forward, turning, swinging), at what speeds, on which kinds of site, and in which light and weather, using data from mine safety and workplace safety agencies in several countries?

facts.text: The research was to identify which heavy-machine collision situations cause the most deaths and serious injuries.
facts.quote: Which situations cause the most deaths and serious injuries

facts.text: The research was to identify which heavy-machine collision situations cause the most property damage.
facts.quote: which cause the most property damage?

facts.text: The research was to investigate operator responses to proximity warnings, including reaction times, ignored alarms, alarm fatigue, switching systems off and the false alarm rate operators accept.
facts.quote: What is known about how operators respond to proximity warnings: reaction times, ignored alarms, alarm fatigue and switching systems off, and what false alarm rate operators accept?

facts.text: The research was to investigate normal work tasks that look like collision risks to a sensor, with loading a truck, working beside a wall or stockpile, and working close to ground crew as candidate examples.
facts.quote: Which normal work tasks look like a collision risk to a sensor, for example loading a truck, working beside a wall or a stockpile, or working close to ground crew?

facts.text: The research was to investigate potential new risks from automatic braking on heavy machines: operator injury from a sudden stop, spilled loads, loss of stability on slopes, vehicles following behind, lost productivity and over-reliance on the system.
facts.quote: Which new risks does automatic braking create on heavy machines: operator injury from a sudden stop, spilled loads, loss of stability on slopes, vehicles following behind, lost productivity, and over-reliance on the system?

facts.text: The research was to investigate how operator behavior changes once automatic braking exists.
facts.quote: How does operator behavior change once automatic braking exists?

facts.text: The research was to investigate how human operators are represented in simulation-based testing, including reaction-time models and operator models, and how well those models are validated.
facts.quote: How are human operators represented in simulation-based testing (reaction-time models, operator models), and how well are those models validated?

facts.text: The research ground rules required neutrality toward vendors, products and technologies.
facts.quote: the research was to stay neutral toward vendors, products and technologies.

facts.text: The research ground rules required each important claim to be classified by its evidence: official statistics, peer-reviewed study, industry report, a vendor's own claim or expert opinion.
facts.quote: Each important claim was to be typed by its evidence (official statistics, peer-reviewed study, industry report, a vendor's own claim, or expert opinion)

facts.text: The research ground rules required each data source to carry its date, country and industry.
facts.quote: each data source was to carry its date, country and industry.

facts.text: The research ground rules required findings from on-road driving rather than off-road machines to be flagged as on-road findings.
facts.quote: Findings that come from on-road driving rather than off-road machines were to be flagged as such.

facts.text: The research ground rules required conflicting findings to be reported rather than smoothed over.
facts.quote: Conflicting findings were to be reported rather than smoothed over

facts.text: The research ground rules required unavailable information to be recorded as "not found" rather than replaced with a guessed number.
facts.quote: where something could not be found the research was to write "not found" instead of guessing a number.
